title: Measurement Geometry as a Resource for Certifying Network Nonlocality
abstract: Quantum networks can exhibit nonclassical correlations that cannot be explained by classical models with independent sources. While the role of entanglement is well understood, the impact of measurement design remains largely unexplored. Here we develop an operational framework for certifying network nonlocality in the bilocal Alice--Bob--Charlie network using ancilla-assisted meters to evaluate the nonlocal observables required for bilocal and fully network nonlocal (FNN) witnesses. The approach successfully reproduces both bilocal and FNN correlations in simulation. On the 156-qubit superconducting processor \textit{ibm\_kingston}, we observe bilocal nonlocality with $\mathcal{S}_{\rm BLHV}=1.067(6)>1$ after readout-error mitigation, while the FNN witnesses reach $99\%$ and $96\%$ of their certification thresholds, implying the substantially stronger requirements for FNN certification. We further show that Bob's joint measurement determines the accessible level of network nonlocality: bilocal and FNN certification are optimized by different measurement settings, while both violations can disappear even for maximally entangled states. These results identify measurement geometry as an independent resource for network nonlocality and provide a practical route toward its certification on programmable quantum processors.
summary: This paper introduces an operational method to certify network nonlocality in three-party quantum systems by analyzing the role of measurement geometry. Using superconducting hardware, they successfully demonstrated bilocal nonlocality while showing that the stronger Full Network Nonlocal correlations are significantly harder to detect experimentally. This establishes measurement design as a crucial, independent resource for certifying genuine multipartite quantum correlations.
main_problem: The research aims to develop an operational framework to certify network nonlocality, recognizing that measurement design is an independent resource beyond just the distributed entanglement.
main_result: They successfully demonstrated bilocal nonlocality on a superconducting processor and showed that Full Network Nonlocality (FNN) requires substantially stronger certification than bilocal nonlocality.
method: The framework uses ancilla-assisted meter circuits to evaluate nonlocal observables required for both Bilocal (BLHV) and Fully Network Nonlocal (FNN) witnesses in a three-party quantum network.
model_or_system: The system modeled is the bilocal Alice--Bob--Charlie quantum network, initialized with two independent entangled pairs. The analysis focuses on how Bob's joint measurement determines the accessible level of nonlocality.
key_observables: BLHV witness violation ($S_{BLHV} > 1$) and FNN witnesses ($R_{CNS}, R_{NSC}$ exceeding classical bounds like 3).
important_parameters: The entanglement parameter $	heta$ controlling the initial state, and the measurement geometry parameters $(\varphi, \phi)$ defining Bob's joint measurement.
main_assumptions: The study assumes that measurement geometry can be systematically varied via ancilla-assisted circuits to test for nonlocality resources.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the hierarchy of nonlocality ($	ext{BLHV} \subset 	ext{LHV} \subset 	ext{nonFNN} \subset 	ext{NS}$), the bilocal network setup, and parameter space plots showing how witness violations depend on measurement settings.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical hierarchy of nonlocality models (BLHV vs. FNN), develops an operational framework using ancilla-assisted measurements for both witnesses, simulates results to show FNN is stronger than BLHV, and finally tests these protocols experimentally on a superconducting quantum processor.
why_interesting: It provides concrete experimental pathways for testing complex multipartite correlations (nonlocality) beyond simple entanglement measures, directly relevant to building fault-tolerant quantum communication networks.

BLHV corresponds to independent classical sources, LHV allows shared classical randomness, and nonFNN allows one source to generate arbitrary NS correlations. The quan- tum set (Q) lies between LHV and NS but is incomparable with nonFNN. Violations of BLHV and nonFNN certify bilo- cal network nonlocality and full network nonlocality (FNN), respectively.
